Current Signal (Jul 21, 2026): Conway:WTI is at 33.7% — propane at Conway now priced at just 33.7 cents for every dollar of crude oil value per gallon as WTI climbed to $84.91 while propane softened. That ratio sits near the low end of historical observations and well below the historical average of ~46%. When both hubs are below their 25th percentile, forward propane purchases have historically delivered above-average value over the following 3–6 months.
Price in Shale-Era Context — Is Propane Actually Cheap? 2012–present · 162 months
2012 is the line of demarcation for this industry — the point where shale production and large-scale exports rewrote how propane is priced. These charts plot the distribution of every monthly settlement since, at both hubs, with today's price marked in amber. It's the only era that describes the market as it functions today.

The verdict: Measured against the era we actually live in, today's price sits below the shale-era mean at both hubs — Conway at the 43rd percentile, Mt Belvieu at the 41st. So propane is genuinely soft, on three counts at once: below its era mean in absolute terms, historically cheap relative to crude, and sitting on a record inventory overhang. The supply picture supporting that softness has real staying power — US natural gas production should remain elevated for years as LNG export demand keeps pulling gas through processing, and the damaged Persian Gulf LNG infrastructure has only lengthened that runway. This is a market where the fundamentals and the relative-value signal are pointing the same direction at once.

Analyst Narrative — Current Market Context
Supply Structure
Production is running at ~2.99M bbl/wk — up 16% vs 2023. But exports have absorbed nearly all that growth, running at 55–88% of production. The structural story: US propane is now a globally-traded commodity with domestic retail competing directly against Asian crackers and European heating demand.
Build Season Risk
The 2026-27 build season is at 22.8M bbls through week 16, with four draws across the season (Apr 24, May 1, May 22, Jul 3). The +6.3M build this week was the largest single-week build of the season and drove cumulative pace to within 7M of the 5yr avg (29.8M). Light exports (1.573M / 54.4%) were the direct cause. The Projection sheet projects a season peak of 113.8M bbls (base case), which would be a record high — but slow build rates are the bullish offset. A normal winter on top of a record-high start could still stress supply by February.
Hormuz Factor
WTI climbed to $84.91 as of Jul 21 — the highest level since the post-Hormuz recovery began. C3:WTI ratios compressed to 33-36% as crude rallied and propane softened, reaching the lowest ratio reading of the season. The record 99.8M inventory print provides no floor support. Persian Gulf production capacity (Ras Laffan, Ju'aymah) remains offline for years regardless of the Hormuz shipping reopening. Watch for Indian buyers returning to the US FOB market as the reality of sustained Gulf supply shortfalls becomes clear.
Structural Forces Reshaping Global LPG Markets — 2026 and Beyond
⚠
Persian Gulf Infrastructure Damage
Feb–Apr 2026
The US-Israeli conflict with Iran beginning February 28, 2026 triggered a cascade of energy infrastructure damage across the Persian Gulf.

Ras Laffan, Qatar
Iranian missile strikes March 18–19 damaged LNG Trains 4 and 6, cutting Qatar's LNG export capacity by ~17% (12.8 MTPA). Qatar's LPG exports — ~13% of shipments — also impacted. Force majeure declared to buyers in China, South Korea, Italy and Belgium. Annual revenue loss: $20 billion.

Ju'aymah LPG Terminal, Saudi Arabia
Fires impacted LPG and NGL exports as of April 9. Saudi propane and butane exports halted for multiple weeks following earlier strikes on Ras Tanura.

South Pars / Asaluyeh, Iran
Israeli strikes March 18 damaged 12% of Iran's total gas production, halting two refineries with combined capacity of 100 million cubic meters per day.

Strait of Hormuz
Effectively closed through late May 2026. Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Qatar and Bahrain collectively shut in 10.5 million barrels per day of crude oil production in April. Brent peaked at $138/bbl on April 7.
⏱
Recovery Timeline — Years, Not Months
Equipment constrained
The defining constraint on Persian Gulf LPG supply recovery is not capital — it is equipment lead times.

Ras Laffan: 3–5 years
Replacement gas turbines for refrigeration compressors face global delivery delays of 2–4 years. Only three manufacturers globally produce the large-frame turbines required. These suppliers entered 2026 with order books already stretched by data center expansion and coal plant retirements. Rystad Energy estimates total regional repair costs at $25+ billion.

Iran's South Pars
Iran's exclusion from Western supply chains means reliance on Chinese and domestic contractors — slower and more expensive. No credible timeline for full restoration.

Saudi facilities
Some may resume within months, but Ju'aymah LPG terminal damage timeline remains unclear.

The bottom line
Nearly half of Asia's propane imports in 2025 came from the Persian Gulf. That supply gap is structural — not temporary — and Asian buyers are actively rerouting to US supply for the medium term.
📈
US Production — Structurally Elevated
Record highs forecast
Approximately 70–80% of US propane production is derived from the natural gas processing stream. When raw natural gas is processed at gas plants, propane is extracted as a byproduct NGL before the methane moves on to pipelines or LNG export terminals. The remaining 20–30% comes from crude oil refining.

This means propane supply is a direct function of how much natural gas the US produces and processes — and that number is going structurally higher. The EIA forecasts US marketed natural gas production will reach record highs of 120.8 Bcf/d in 2026 and 122.3 Bcf/d in 2027, driven by the Permian, Haynesville and Appalachia regions.

The LNG Export Multiplier
Five new LNG export projects start through 2027, adding ~6 Bcf/d of capacity. Each Bcf/d of new LNG export capacity incentivizes additional upstream gas drilling. That incremental gas runs through processing plants where propane is extracted from the gas stream. More gas wells → more processing → more propane. The EIA forecasts propane production to grow 4% in 2026 and 6% in 2027.

These trends don't reverse quickly — the wells are drilled, the processing infrastructure is built, and the LNG export commitments are signed. Propane supply from the natural gas stream is effectively locked in at elevated levels for the foreseeable future.
🚢
VLGC Fleet — The Shipping Constraint
Why weekly data is noisy
Very Large Gas Carriers (VLGCs) are the sole vessels capable of moving propane economically on long-haul US-to-Asia routes. The global fleet is finite — approximately 370–390 active VLGCs worldwide, with an orderbook of ~27% of existing fleet delivering through 2027–28. Fleet growth is accelerating — 7% in 2026, peaking at 16% in 2027 — but new vessels take years to build and deploy.

Why your weekly EIA export number is inherently noisy
A standard VLGC carries approximately 500,000–550,000 barrels of propane per voyage. At current US export rates of ~12–15 VLGC loadings per week, a single vessel delayed by 2–3 days — berth congestion, weather, Panama Canal slot timing — moves the weekly EIA print by 500K+ barrels. The late-May swing between 2.625M and 1.649M bbls in consecutive weeks was a clean example; June prints have settled into a steadier ~2.0M bbls/week range, with the 4-week average holding near 2.09M.

The Cape of Good Hope factor
Panama Canal auction fees hit record highs in April 2026 — some slots reportedly fetching $4 million. A growing share of US-to-Asia cargoes now route via Cape of Good Hope instead, adding ~14 days to each voyage (30 days → 44 days). Longer voyages mean ships return to load less frequently, creating lumpier scheduling patterns and wider week-to-week export variance. Houston–Chiba VLGC freight surged ~55% month-over-month in April 2026, reaching near $290/metric ton.

The right way to read the data
The 4-week rolling average is the minimum smoothing window needed to filter vessel timing noise. Even that can be distorted if a cluster of ships all slipped the same week. The reliable signal is the 8–12 week trend direction — not any single weekly print. A one-week spike or drop almost always reflects ship scheduling, not a change in Asian demand for US propane.
US Export Infrastructure — Capacity Expanding Precisely When Asia Needs It New terminals online 2026
Enterprise Neches River Terminal
Shipped its first cargo in April 2026, ahead of its originally planned June launch. Phase 2 allows up to 360,000 bbl/day of propane loading capacity. The early startup directly captured diverted Asian demand as Hormuz closed.
Energy Transfer Nederland
250,000 bbl/day flex capacity brought online July 2025 has been fully deployed for LPG exports. Enterprise Houston terminal 300,000 bbl/day expansion expected later in 2026. Terminal fees surged from 8.6¢/gal in January to 44¢/gal by end of Q1 — a 5× increase. By June, July cargo offers were reportedly trading near cancellation levels once Panama Canal transit costs were factored in, with Indian buyers pausing in anticipation of a Hormuz reopening.
Global LPG trade rebalancing
Global seaborne LPG exports recovered to 4.8 million bbl/day in May 2026, led by the US. Supply remains ~600,000 bbl/day below February 2026 record highs. India, hit hardest by Persian Gulf supply loss, now relies heavily on US cargoes. The Mont Belvieu propane-ethane spread reached $325/ton on May 12, incentivizing propane over ethane at flexible terminals.
Strategic Implications for Retail Propane Markets The retail takeaway
Export Demand Pull
Asian buyers replacing Persian Gulf supply with US propane for the next 3–5 years. This structurally competes with domestic storage builds — every barrel exported is a barrel not in a tank in Kansas or Iowa. The weak 2026-27 build season pace (59% below 5-year average) is partly a direct consequence.
Production Baseline
Record US gas production means propane supply is not going to tighten from the production side. The only mechanism that tightens domestic supply is exports absorbing an increasing share — which is exactly what is happening and will continue for years. High domestic inventory is the buffer, but it is being drawn down faster than normal build rates replenish it.
The Forward Buying Window
Record inventory and C3:WTI ratios near the 18th–23rd percentile of their seasonal range still mark a historically favorable forward buying window, even after the Hormuz-driven crude selloff lifted the ratio off its springtime lows. But the export structural shift means this window is finite. As Persian Gulf supply stays offline for years, sustained Asian demand for US propane will keep pressure on domestic builds — and the window between spot value and forward risk may narrow sooner than a pure inventory analysis suggests.

The Setup — A Genuine "Super" Event Demand headwind
A strong El Niño pushes the polar jet north and parks the Pacific jet across the South. That tilts the northern tier — your Great Lakes, Ohio Valley and Northeast demand centers — toward a milder, lower-degree-day winter, while the southern tier turns cool, wet and cloudy.

The two historical bookends point the same way: 2015–16 (peak ~+2.6°C) cut national HDDs 12% and propane demand 16%. The record 1877–78 event left North America so mild it was called the "year without a winter."

The pattern is the point. Even in strong events the warm signal's exact footprint shifts year to year. The direction is reliable; the magnitude in any one state is not.

Key Regional Nuances Don't read regions as monolithic
Midwest sub-gradient
Upper Midwest & Great Lakes (MN/WI/MI): –12 to –18%. Chicago–Indiana–Ohio corridor: –8 to –12%. Eastern Kansas & Missouri: –4 to –8%. Treat northern and southern halves as separate demand books.
California exception
A wet, cold-rain regime keeps CA temperatures near to slightly below normal. In a cold-averse population, that pulls propane heat even when the thermometer reads mild. Populated coastal and valley CA can run slightly above normal demand.
TX/OK cold-snap tail risk
A west-QBO / stratospheric setup can punch arctic air and snowstorms into Texas and Oklahoma — sharp demand spikes of 1–2 weeks inside a mild mean. Model as "near-normal mean with tail risk," not "mild and quiet."
Mid-Atlantic coastal storms
The Virginia–Maryland–Delaware corridor is prone to above-normal snowfall in west-QBO El Niño winters. Big coastal-storm demand pulls occur even inside a low-degree-day season. Mild mean, lumpy demand.
What to Plan Around Lower total · higher volatility
Frame the season to dealers as below-normal seasonal demand concentrated in your Midwest, Great Lakes and Northeast core — with California and the South as offsets, and real spike risk to size supply against.
Temperature isn't a lock
Even in strong events the warm signal's footprint shifts year to year. Direction reliable; magnitude in any one state is not.
Lumpy, not quiet
A west-QBO / stratospheric setup can punch arctic air and snowstorms into the central, eastern and southern US — sharp demand spikes inside a mild mean.
Upside-mild scenario
If 2026–27 rivals 1877–78 ("year without a winter"), degree days fall further still. That event's exact magnitude carries large historical data uncertainty — treat as a tail, not a base case.
Spring 2027 second act
Above-normal Midwest precipitation → wet spring → delayed planting/harvest → elevated grain drying demand Apr–May. Buy supply at the March trough before competitors notice.
